thread.title: Berkshire Hathaway Might Have One of the Best Earnings Reports Ever

title: Berkshire Hathaway Might Have One of the Best Earnings Reports Ever

organizations.name: et order reprints lacy o'toole/cnbc/nbcu photo bank

text:
Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway Might Have One of the Best Earnings Reports Ever This Weekend By Nov. 1, 2018 6:00 a.m. ET Order Reprints Lacy O'Toole/CNBC/NBCU Photo Bank via Getty Images Text size
Berkshire Hathaway ’s third-quarter results, due on Saturday morning, could show enormous net income of about $19 billion—close to a record for any company—due largely to big unrealized gains in Berkshire’s $200 billion equity portfolio.
Barclays analyst Jay Gelb estimates that Berkshire (ticker: BRK.A) earned $18.8 billion in the third quarter, up from $4.1 billion in the year-earlier period. Berkshire’s Class A shares were up $2,126, or 0.7%, on Wednesday to $307,705, and have gained 3.4% so far this year.
Apple (AAPL), the world’s most profitable company, earned $20.1 billion in the quarter ended in December 2017, which is believed to be the most-profitable quarter of any company ever. It is expected to have had net income of $13.5 billion in the September quarter. ( Those results are due after the close of trading on Thursday. )
Investors aren’t likely to get too excited about Berkshire’s total earnings because they reflect a new accounting rule that took effect this year that requires Berkshire and other companies to include unrealized investment gains in their quarterly profits. Berkshire had more than $12.7 billion of investment gains in the period, mostly unrealized, Gelb estimates. The gains should reflect paper profits in such big Berkshire equity holdings as Apple and Bank of America (BAC) in the third quarter.
Berkshire CEO Warren Buffett warned shareholders in its annual letter earlier this year that the new rule would lead to “wild and capricious” swings in earnings and that the “ ‘bottom line’ will be useless.” Investors, he said, should focus on the operating results excluding the investment swings.

In addition to the earnings, investors will be focused on Berkshire’s stock-buyback activity in the third quarter. Gelb sees about $500 million in buybacks.
Berkshire loosened the constraints on its repurchase program in early August and gave Buffett and Vice Chairman Charlie Munger the ability to repurchase stock when they deemed the shares to be trading below their estimate of intrinsic value, “conservatively determined.” Under the old rules, Berkshire could pay no more than 1.2 times book value. The company repurchased no stock in recent years because the stock consistently traded above that level.
Read more: IBM and Berkshire Hathaway Highlight the Risk of Counting on Stock Buybacks
The repurchases will be an indication of Buffett’s enthusiasm for Berkshire shares. He told CNBC in an interview on Aug. 30—his 88th birthday—that Berkshire had bought “some” stock after it got the more flexible authorization, but he didn’t provide a figure.
Analysts and investors expect that Berkshire moved cautiously on buybacks initially. Berkshire bulls are hoping that Buffett uses the new authority to aggressively repurchase the stock in the future with its enormous cash position of more than $100 billion. Buffett, however, has long been lukewarm to share repurchases at Berkshire and has bought back virtually no stock. Newsletter Sign-up
The headline earnings for the quarter are likely to generate attention due to the new accounting rule. However, the operating results excluding investment gains (realized and unrealized) are more important. Gelb expects strong operating earnings of $3,718 per Class A share, up 78% from the year-earlier period, helped by the better insurance results. Catastrophe losses were high a year ago due to several major hurricanes.
Berkshire’s book value ended the second quarter at about $218,000 per Class A share, and Gelb sees third-quarter book at nearly $229,000 a share. That would leave Berkshire trading at a reasonable 1.35 times book value. Barron’s has been favorable on Berkshire .
The stock market lost ground in October, with the S&P 500 off about 7%. That may have depressed Berkshire’s equity portfolio, but it probably bested the market, with Coca-Cola (KO) and Wells Fargo (WFC)—two big Berkshire holdings—higher in the month and Apple falling about 2%.
Here’s what Buffett wrote about the new accounting rule in his shareholder letter:
“The new rule says that the net change in unrealized investment gains and losses in stocks we hold must be included in all net income figures we report to you. That requirement will produce some truly wild and capricious swings in our GAAP bottom-line. Berkshire owns $170 billion of marketable stocks (not including our shares of Kraft Heinz [KHC]), and the value of these holdings can easily swing by $10 billion or more within a quarterly reporting period. Including gyrations of that magnitude in reported net income will swamp the truly important numbers that describe our operating performance. For analytical purposes, Berkshire’s ‘bottom line’ will be useless.”
